profane

/pruh-FAYN/ - rhymes with plain · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Profane means irreverent toward the sacred or solemn; laced with cursing.

The dictation app transcribed the plumber's profane muttering faithfully, and the emailed invoice arrived unprintable.

Example

Grandmother's table had one law: nothing profane between grace and dessert. Uncles who forgot found the swear jar waiting by the gravy boat, and its tariff doubled on Sundays.

Profane covers two kinds of line-crossing: language too coarse for polite company, and treatment of sacred things without the reverence they are owed — its oldest sense is simply 'outside the temple.' This unit's ribald sits nearby but narrower: ribald is crude for laughs, while profane can be crude in dead earnest.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

indecent: Indecent means offending standards of decency — too explicit or improper for the setting, with no humor required. Profane cuts along different lines: coarse, swearing language, or irreverence toward what is sacred. A crude photograph is indecent; cursing in a sanctuary is profane, and neither has to involve the other.

crude: Crude means rough and unrefined — language or manners that skip politeness without necessarily breaking any deeper rule. Profane goes further on two fronts: its coarseness rises to actual cursing, and it can violate the sacred itself. A crude joke is merely impolite; profane speech swears or desecrates.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

pious: devoutly respectful of the sacred

decent: safely inside the bounds of good taste

Where it sits · how grave the disrespect grows

irreverent → profane → blasphemous

irreverent vs. profane: Irreverent is milder than profane — it smirks at solemn things but keeps its language clean.

blasphemous vs. profane: Blasphemous is graver than profane: profane speech disrespects the sacred at large, while blasphemy insults the divine directly and by name.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pro-: before, outside (Latin)

Root — fane: temple (from Latin fanum)

Put it together: Pro- (before, outside) + fane (temple — Latin fanum, and an old English word for a shrine in its own right) = outside the temple. What stood outside the temple was unconsecrated, common ground; profane began as 'not sacred' and slid toward 'offensive to the sacred' — and to polite ears generally.

Use the root in a new word: fanatic: Latin fanaticus gave English the word fanatic - by the 1600s, pamphlet writers were already flinging it at their political rivals.
